questions.question: A retrospective produces three actions: be more proactive about surfacing risk, improve documentation, and communicate earlier with support. Why will these change nothing?
options: They were not assigned to individual owners with due dates
They are intentions; none can block anything, fire on anything, or be checked by anyone
They were written at the end of the meeting when attention was low
They repeat items from previous retrospectives, so the team has stopped believing them
questions.explanation: A system change takes one of four forms — rule, interface, threshold, or capability — and each is verifiable. Option A is the standard fix teams reach for, and it is the most tempting: assigning an owner and a date to "be more proactive" produces an owned intention, which still cannot block or fire on anything.

questions.question: After an incident where an AI feature assigned wrong action owners, the team corrects the affected summaries and closes the retrospective. What is missing?
options: Nothing; the problem is resolved and users are no longer affected
A root-cause analysis document explaining the model's behaviour
A system change, because the correction repaired the instance and left the mechanism that produced it in place
Communication to the affected accounts about what happened
questions.explanation: Repair removes the problem; improvement prevents the next occurrence, catches it earlier, or makes it cheaper. Option A is what the board actually looks like after a competent incident response, and it is exactly the substitution the lesson names: the same incident returns at the next exposure stage with different details.

questions.question: A team repeatedly ships confused metric definitions. The retrospective adopts a rule: "every metric definition must be reviewed before use." Nobody on the team owns metric definitions or has written one. What happens?
options: The rule works, because review forces the team to build the skill over time
The rule is followed sincerely and does not work, because it stands in for a missing capability
The rule works if the review is assigned to the most senior person available
The rule fails because it lacks a threshold that specifies which metrics require review
questions.explanation: Before writing a rule, ask whether anyone can comply with it. Here the gap is capability, and a rule that mandates a review nobody can perform produces a signed-off definition that is still wrong. Option A is the tempting one, because rules sometimes do build habits; but a review by people who cannot evaluate the object teaches nothing and adds a step.

questions.question: A team adopts a well-designed operating rule after a genuine failure. What must be added for the rule not to become process debt?
options: A written rationale so future members understand why it exists
An exception process for cases the rule does not fit
A named enforcer with authority to apply it consistently
A removal review date and the evidence that would retire it
questions.explanation: Rules accumulate, and every rule in a paralysing pile was justified when written. A rule adopted with no condition for removal is debt with no repayment schedule. Option B is the answer most process-aware teams give, and exceptions are useful — but an exception process makes a bad rule survivable rather than removable, which is how the pile grows.

questions.question: A one-off failure occurred because a contractor with unusual access misconfigured an environment during a week that will not repeat. The team drafts a new approval step. What is the correct judgment?
options: Record the incident and change nothing, because the condition will not recur
Adopt the approval step; approvals are cheap and prevent a class of error
Adopt a threshold instead, so the misconfiguration would be detected automatically
Adopt the step but scope it to contractors only, limiting the cost
questions.explanation: Two tests apply: would the change have prevented the problem, and will the condition recur. Here the second fails, so the rule costs forever and prevents nothing. Option D is the sophisticated-looking compromise and the most tempting, because narrowing scope feels like managing the cost — but a narrow rule guarding a condition that will not return is still permanent overhead.
